description: Virtual Noise Scaling (VNS) changes how the outcomes of noise-amplified circuits are combined, rather than how the noise is amplified. Mitigation schemes based on agnostic noise amplification (KIK and its layered variant, folding-based ZNE, probabilistic error amplification) execute a family of circuits with amplification factors 1, 3, 5, ... and take a linear combination of the measured expectation values. The coefficients follow from a Taylor expansion of the noise inverse around the zero-noise point \(s = 1\).

The observation behind VNS is that \(s = 1\) is a poor expansion point. The eigenvalues of the noise operator lie in \((0, 1]\), so the expansion is centered at the edge of the distribution rather than inside it. The mitigation function that maps noise eigenvalues back to 1 has a plateau whose width grows with the mitigation order, and that plateau extends past \(s = 1\). Rescaling the noise operator by a constant \(g\), which amounts to \(K \to gK\) and \(K_I \to gK_I\) in the mitigation coefficients, slides the eigenvalue distribution into the middle of the plateau.

The gain is in sampling cost, not bias: a given mitigated infidelity is reached at a lower mitigation order, and therefore at far lower runtime overhead. Because the rescaling happens in post-processing, it can be applied to data that has already been collected; the scaling factor \(g\) is itself read off from the measured noise-amplified expectation values.

VNS composes with layered mitigation, where the circuit is sliced into layers that are amplified and mitigated separately. Layering is not always worth it, and the crossover is circuit-independent: it depends only on the smallest eigenvalue \(s_{\min}\) of the noise operator and on the number of layers. Two layers beat one below \(s_{\min} \simeq 0.65\) (that is, for stronger noise), with a further two-to-three-layer crossover near \(s_{\min} \simeq 0.5\). Above the threshold the extra layers cost more than they save.
how_it_works: Execute the noise-amplified circuits of the underlying agnostic amplification scheme, for example \(K(K_I K)^k\) for \(k = 0, 1, \ldots, m\).
Estimate the scaling factor \(g\) from the measured amplified expectation values, choosing it so the noise eigenvalue interval \([g s_{\min}, g]\) sits on the plateau of the mitigation function.
Recompute the linear-combination coefficients \(a_k(g)\) from the Taylor expansion recentered by \(g\), instead of the Richardson coefficients.
Combine the measured expectation values with the new coefficients to obtain the mitigated estimate.
Decide whether to mitigate in layers by comparing \(s_{\min}\) against the layer-count threshold: below roughly 0.65, split into two layers and apply VNS to each.

Rescaled noise spectrum (s_min = smallest eigenvalue of the noise operator)
Layer-count threshold for two-layer mitigation
key_equations.latex: s_{\min} \lesssim 0.65 \implies \text{two layers cost less than one}

advantages: Pure post-processing: no new circuits, no noise characterization, and applicable to already-collected data

Reduces runtime overhead by orders of magnitude in the strong-noise regime; combined with two-layer mitigation, from \(3.6 \times 10^8\) to \(3.8 \times 10^4\) at a mitigated infidelity of 0.024 in the reported analysis
Keeps the drift resilience of agnostic noise amplification, since no noise model is learned
Applies to any constant-step amplification factors, so it covers KIK, folding ZNE and probabilistic error amplification alike
Gives a circuit-independent rule for when layered mitigation pays off
Compatible with dynamic circuits, error detection and error correction, and with mid-circuit measurement and preparation error mitigation
disadvantages: Applies only to agnostic noise amplification schemes; it does not help probabilistic error cancellation
The scaling factor must be estimated, and a poor estimate moves the eigenvalues off the plateau
The layer-count threshold is derived from an upper bound on the two-layer infidelity, so the actual crossover can differ for a specific circuit
Layering below the threshold increases rather than decreases the sampling overhead
Sampling overhead still grows with circuit volume; the reduction is a large constant factor, not a change in scaling
